newsitem.title: USA: Fed says wages rising despite slowing U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: Fed says wages rising despite slowing U.S. economy.

text.p: Pressure for wage increases is rising across the country despite a somewhat slower pace of economic growth, the Federal Reserve said Wednesday.
In its latest summary of national economic activity, the central bank described labour markets throughout much of the country as "tight" and noted "some proliferation" of wage increases.

The latest national summary, known as the Beige Book, was prepared by the Minneapolis Fed district bank based on interviews with business officials in all 12 Fed districts from mid-September through Oct. 22.
"Indications of upward pressure on wages continue to spread geographically and to grow in terms of affected occupations and ranges of skill levels," the Fed summary said.

That picture contrasted with a government report on Tuesday that said that wages grew more slowly in the third quarter as employers' labour costs advanced only 0.6 percent after a 0.8 percent rise in the second quarter.

That report fuelled a rally in financial markets that carried long-term interest rates sharply lower on Tuesday. Rates on the 30-year Treasury rose a bit to 6.70 percent Wednesday, from 6.68 percent on Tuesday, after the Fed's report of rising wage demands.
Despite the stepped-up pressure on wages, the Fed saw little indication of a pickup in price inflation.
"In contrast to some proliferation of wage increases, reports of price increases for raw materials, goods and services remain limited," the Fed said.
The Fed said economic growth was moderate across much of the United States during the fall, though the pace has slowed in some regions, notably the Southwest and much of the Eastern Seaboard.
"Moderate expansion of business activity characterises the economy in most Federal Reserve districts," the Fed said, "But on balance the pace of growth reportedly has slowed somewhat."

The Commerce Department earlier Wednesday said the economy grew at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the third quarter, off from the brisk 4.7 percent rate in the second quarter, partly because of a big drop in consumer spending.

For its part, the central bank said consumer spending was moderate. "There are some signs of strength, but no areas where sales are booming," the Fed summary said. Consumers account for about two-thirds of the economy through purchases of goods and services.
The key automobile sector was called "mixed." Sales were strong in the Fed's Minneapolis district but slowed in the region covered by the Dallas Fed.

Manufacturing industries varied by region but on balance were "largely stable to stronger," the Fed said. Inventories were "generally normal to somewhat below normal, and show little indication of either production bottlenecks or of weakening demand," it added.

The Commerce Department said business inventories swelled in the third quarter at the fastest pace in 18 months, climbing at an annual rate of nearly $40 billion. Analysts said that might dampen growth in the fourth quarter until stocks are brought into line with output.
Construction activity was strong in several Fed regions, but slacker in a few. Rising demand for apartments was spurring new construction in New York, an area that has been dormant for years.
However, building slowed in the Southeast, including in Atlanta where construction had been boosted by preparations for the summer Olympics.
Farmers were enjoying better times than had been expected just a few months ago when drought hit the Southwest and cold, wet weather delayed planting in the Midwest.
"The 1996 crop is turning out better than many anticipated this spring," the Fed said.
